value.overview: The Comb Duck, also called the American Comb Duck, is a large, distinctive waterfowl species of tropical South America. It belongs to the duck family Anatidae and is named for the fleshy knob or comb on the male’s bill. It uses freshwater wetlands, flooded grasslands, marshes, lakes, rivers, and nearby agricultural areas. Although its normal range is South American, it is recorded only rarely in Costa Rica, where it is treated as an accidental or very rare visitor.
value.classification: The Comb Duck is an anseriform waterfowl in the family Anatidae. Its scientific name is Sarkidiornis sylvicola; it is separate from the closely related African and Asian Knob-billed Duck, Sarkidiornis melanotos.
value.identification: This is a large duck with a white head and neck marked by dark spots, glossy blue-black upperparts, and dark flanks. The male is considerably larger than the female and develops a prominent black, fleshy knob on the upper bill during the breeding season. Females have a smaller or poorly developed knob. In flight, the contrasting white body and dark wings are noticeable. Immature birds are duller and may lack the strongly developed bill knob.
value.rangeHabitat: The Comb Duck’s regular range extends across tropical South America, from Colombia and Venezuela south through the Amazon and eastern lowlands to Paraguay, southeastern Brazil, and northeastern Argentina. It occupies freshwater marshes, seasonally flooded savannas, quiet lakes, slow rivers, ponds, flooded grassland, and sometimes rice fields or other agricultural wetlands. In Costa Rica it is not a regular resident or breeder. The species is listed as accidental or very rare, with records mainly involving lowland wetlands, including Guanacaste.
value.migrationStatus: The species is largely resident, but it can make local or seasonal movements in response to rainfall, flooding, and water availability. In Costa Rica it is an accidental or very rare visitor, not a regular migrant.
value.breeding: Comb Ducks usually breed near still or slow-moving freshwater. They commonly nest in tree cavities, but may also use tree stumps, abandoned nests, tall grass, or other sheltered sites close to water. The female lays a clutch of pale eggs and normally performs incubation. Nesting behavior can include more than one female laying in a shared nest. Males defend females and young, while nest-site defense is less pronounced. There is no reliable evidence that the species regularly breeds in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is mainly plant-based. Comb Ducks graze or dabble for grasses, sedges, seeds, grains, and soft parts of aquatic plants. They also take aquatic insect larvae, other invertebrates, and occasionally small aquatic animals. Feeding occurs in shallow water, wet grassland, muddy margins, and cultivated fields such as rice-growing areas. The species may feed by day and often rests or perches in trees near wetlands.
value.behavior: Comb Ducks are strong swimmers and can also walk and graze on land. They often occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups, although larger concentrations may form where food and water are abundant. They regularly perch in trees and roost near wetlands. Their movements are influenced by seasonal flooding and drying. Males are conspicuous because of their large size and bill knob, while females and immature birds can appear less boldly patterned.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population trend is not well established. The species is not currently considered globally threatened, although it is locally uncommon and has a scattered distribution in parts of its range.
